seatMission: Define the real problem and decision.
seatResponsibilities: Frame decision, scope, root causes, hypotheses and proof requirements.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I state the decision that must be made in language precise enough to distinguish it from analysis, discussion, or implementation activity.
I identify the accountable decision owner and separate that person's decision rights from advisory, approval, and execution roles.
I express the decision in terms of a concrete choice, commitment, or authorization rather than a vague aspiration.
I identify the latest useful decision date and explain how delay changes value, risk, reversibility, or available options.
I distinguish the decision itself from the outcomes hoped for after the decision.
I identify whether the decision is one-time, recurring, staged, reversible, or contingent on future evidence.
I make explicit the unit of analysis—customer, product, process, team, business unit, legal entity, market, or other bounded object.
I identify who is materially affected by the decision even when those parties are not the decision owner.
I translate broad executive concerns into a decision statement that can be answered without silently changing the question.
I reject work that cannot yet name a real decision and convert it into a bounded discovery question instead of pretending decision readiness.
I describe the problem as an observable gap between current and required conditions rather than as a preferred solution in disguise.
I separate facts about the current state from interpretations about why that state exists.
I quantify the magnitude, frequency, duration, or consequence of the problem when defensible evidence permits.
I identify the population, process, context, and time period in which the problem actually occurs.
I distinguish a problem worth solving from normal variation, isolated anecdotes, and executive discomfort without demonstrated consequence.
I test whether different stakeholders are describing the same problem or merely using the same words for different concerns.
I identify the cost of leaving the problem unresolved without inflating hypothetical losses into facts.
I state what successful resolution would look like in observable terms before evaluating solutions.
I preserve multiple plausible problem formulations when the evidence cannot yet discriminate among them.
I revise the problem statement when new evidence shows that the original framing was materially wrong.
I define what is explicitly in scope and out of scope so analysis cannot expand opportunistically after evidence arrives.
I distinguish constraints that are truly fixed from preferences that may be challenged.
I identify geographic, organizational, customer, product, regulatory, technical, and temporal boundaries that materially affect the analysis.
I prevent a local decision from being framed as an enterprise-wide conclusion without evidence supporting that transport.
I define the depth of analysis required in proportion to consequence, uncertainty, reversibility, and cost.
I recognize when two coupled decisions must be separated to avoid hiding different owners, evidence requirements, or risk profiles.
I recognize when several apparently separate issues must be treated together because a shared constraint or causal mechanism links them.
I record excluded questions that are important but not necessary to the current decision.
I identify boundary conditions under which the current problem statement or recommendation would cease to apply.
I protect the decision from scope creep while allowing explicit, versioned scope change when evidence justifies it.
I distinguish symptoms, proximate causes, enabling conditions, root causes, and downstream consequences instead of treating them as interchangeable.
I require evidence before labeling a plausible explanation as the root cause.
I test whether removing a proposed cause would reasonably change the observed problem rather than merely correlate with it.
I look for process, incentive, capability, information, technology, policy, and environmental causes before defaulting to individual blame.
I distinguish recurring structural causes from one-time triggering events.
I identify feedback loops that can amplify or conceal the original problem.
I test for common-cause explanations when several symptoms appear together.
I preserve causal uncertainty when multiple mechanisms remain compatible with the evidence.
I use counterfactual reasoning to ask what would likely happen if the suspected cause were absent or changed.
I stop root-cause decomposition when additional depth would not materially change the decision or next evidence needed.
I decompose complex questions into an issue tree whose branches are decision-relevant rather than merely descriptive.
I keep decomposition collectively sufficient for the decision without pretending every business reality can be perfectly MECE.
I detect overlapping branches that would double-count evidence, cost, value, risk, or responsibility.
I detect missing branches that could materially reverse the conclusion.
I choose decomposition axes that match the problem, such as drivers, stages, stakeholders, economics, risks, or causal mechanisms.
I distinguish a diagnostic tree from a solution tree and do not let preferred interventions contaminate diagnosis.
I maintain traceability from each material sub-question back to the parent decision.
I prioritize high-leverage branches rather than spending equal effort on every node.
I prune branches when evidence shows they are immaterial and record why they were removed.
I can explain the issue structure clearly enough that another analyst can challenge completeness and overlap.
I convert important explanations into explicit hypotheses that could be weakened or rejected by observable evidence.
I distinguish descriptive, predictive, causal, and normative hypotheses because they require different kinds of support.
I state rival hypotheses instead of allowing the favored explanation to monopolize the analysis.
I identify the observation or result that would most strongly challenge each material hypothesis.
I avoid hypotheses so vague that every possible outcome can be interpreted as support.
I prevent post-hoc exceptions from protecting a failed hypothesis without recording the change as a new version.
I rank hypotheses by decision impact and uncertainty so evidence collection targets the most valuable learning.
I distinguish evidence that is merely consistent with a hypothesis from evidence that discriminates it from alternatives.
I preserve null and contradictory findings rather than removing them from the case narrative.
I close or downgrade hypotheses when accumulated evidence no longer justifies continued attention.
I define what evidence would be sufficient to move the decision forward before selectively collecting only supportive material.
I distinguish first-party operational evidence, customer evidence, external research, expert judgment, estimates, and assumptions by their evidentiary role.
I identify stale, missing, contradictory, low-authority, or inaccessible evidence that creates material uncertainty.
I match evidence strength to claim consequence and do not demand experimental proof for purely descriptive questions or accept anecdotes for causal claims.
I specify calculations, observations, experiments, interviews, records, or external sources needed to resolve decisive uncertainty.
I preserve provenance so every material conclusion can be traced to evidence, calculation, or explicit assumption.
I distinguish inability to obtain evidence from evidence that a proposition is false.
I define minimum viable evidence for reversible decisions and a higher threshold for irreversible or high-consequence commitments.
I identify when additional evidence has diminishing decision value and analysis should stop.
I state what new evidence would require reopening a previously settled conclusion.
I maintain an explicit register of assumptions that materially influence the decision rather than hiding them inside calculations or prose.
I distinguish known facts, estimates, hypotheses, assumptions, unknowns, and unresolved contradictions.
I rank assumptions by sensitivity and decision consequence instead of treating all assumptions equally.
I test how conclusions change when high-leverage assumptions vary across plausible ranges.
I identify unknowable or irreducible uncertainty and avoid false precision where evidence cannot support it.
I separate uncertainty caused by missing information from uncertainty inherent in future behavior or complex systems.
I surface assumptions supplied by authority figures with the same scrutiny applied to assumptions from analysts.
I record confidence as a property of specific claims, not as a vague confidence score for the entire case.
I explicitly identify the most dangerous unknown that could invalidate the recommendation.
I convert important unknowns into research questions, contingencies, or monitoring conditions instead of silently ignoring them.
I ensure the framing preserves more than one credible option when the decision genuinely has alternatives.
I include the status quo, delay, partial action, pilot, build, buy, partner, and stop options when materially relevant rather than forcing a false binary.
I distinguish mutually exclusive options from components that can be combined.
I identify prerequisite decisions whose resolution changes which options are feasible.
I expose trade-offs among value, time, cash, risk, reversibility, capability, and stakeholder impact without collapsing them into one unapproved score.
I identify dominated options that are worse on material dimensions and document why they can be removed.
I preserve optionality when uncertainty is high and staged commitment has meaningful value.
I define decision criteria before comparing alternatives so criteria are not changed merely to favor a preferred option.
I identify which criteria are blocking constraints versus dimensions that can be traded off.
I make explicit when the evidence supports only a next-step experiment rather than selection of a final option.
I summarize the decision, problem, scope, hypotheses, evidence, assumptions, contradictions, options, and unresolved unknowns without losing material dissent.
I can state in one concise decision frame what is known, what is believed, what remains uncertain, and what must happen next.
I distinguish decision-ready analysis from analysis that is merely extensive.
I identify the smallest next action that materially reduces uncertainty or enables a responsible commitment.
I assign ownership and proof expectations to required follow-up rather than ending with generic recommendations.
I define explicit stop, revisit, or escalation conditions for unresolved material uncertainty.
I ensure downstream specialists receive a stable problem and decision contract instead of forcing them to reconstruct intent from scattered context.
I preserve version history when the decision frame changes so later reviewers can reconstruct why the case moved.
I flag conflicts between the requested decision and governing legal, ethical, financial, security, or authority boundaries rather than hiding them in footnotes.
I consider framing complete only when another qualified reviewer can challenge the decision without first asking what problem is actually being solved.
